prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Let’s get this straight: Charles Graner is not America. America would never hold a knife to his wife’s throat, then say when she woke that he was considering killing her. And America’s wife in turn would never call her husband “my own Hannibal Lecter.” Am I right, or what? Charles Graner may be Hannibal Lecter, but he is not America. America is not that kind of husband. Nor would America email his adolescent children photos of himself torturing naked Iraqi prisoners and say “look what Daddy gets to do!” Am I right? America is not that kind of father. America would never torture naked Iraqi prisoners. Let’s be absolutely clear about all of this. And America’s ex-lover and co-defendant would never whisper to the sketch artist at America’s trial: “You forgot the horns.” Charles Graner may or may not have horns, but America is horn-free. America does not torture prisoners. America may render them, fully clothed, to Egypt or Syria, for further interrogation, or to men like Charles Graner, but America is not, ipso facto, Egypt or Syria, and Charles Graner is not now nor has he ever been America. And don’t talk to me about Guantanamo. Please! Let’s get this straight. You and I know who America is. We know what America does and doesn’t do, because we (not Charles Graner!) are America. Am I right? Is this all clear? Tell me—am I right, or what?

Keywords: Let, Charles, Graner

outputs.L1:
Let’s be clear: Charles Graner is not America. America would never hold a knife to his wife’s throat and then, when she awoke, tell her that he had been considering killing her. Nor would America’s wife call her husband “my own Hannibal Lecter.” Am I right, or what?

America may render them—fully clothed—to Egypt or Syria for further interrogation, or deliver them to men like Charles Graner. But America is not, *ipso facto*, Egypt or Syria, and Charles Graner is not now, nor has he ever been, America.

And don’t talk to me about Guantanamo. Please. Let’s get this straight: you and I know who America is. We know what America does and does not do because we—not Charles Graner—are America. Am I right? Is all of this clear? Tell me: am I right, or what?
outputs.L2:
To be perfectly plain, Charles Graner does not represent America. America would not press a knife against his wife’s neck and, after she regained consciousness, tell her he had been thinking about murdering her. His wife, likewise, would not describe him as “my own Hannibal Lecter.” Surely we agree. Graner might resemble Hannibal Lecter, but he is not America. That is not how America behaves as a husband.

Neither would America send his teenage children photographs showing him abusing naked Iraqi detainees, accompanied by the message, “look what Daddy gets to do!” Correct? America is not such a father. America would never subject unclothed Iraqi prisoners to torture. That distinction must remain unmistakable.

Nor would America’s former lover and fellow defendant lean toward the courtroom sketch artist during his trial and murmur, “You forgot the horns.” Graner may have horns or he may not; America unquestionably has none. America does not torture people in custody. It may transfer them—still dressed—to Egypt or Syria for additional questioning, or hand them over to individuals such as Charles Graner. Yet that does not automatically make America Egypt, Syria, or Graner. Charles Graner is not America and never has been.

And spare me any mention of Guantanamo. Seriously. The point should be obvious: you and I understand what America is. We know what America will and will not do because we—not Charles Graner—are America. Isn’t that so? Have I made it clear enough? Tell me: I’m right, aren’t I?
outputs.L3:
The text sarcastically rejects the claim that Charles Graner’s violent and abusive behavior is representative of America. Graner is portrayed as cruel not only toward Iraqi prisoners but also toward his own family, most disturbingly through his decision to share photographs of prisoner abuse with his children. This conduct is presented as morally abhorrent, yet the author’s sarcasm suggests that simply declaring Graner “un-American” does not absolve the nation of responsibility.

The repeated assertion that “America does not torture prisoners” is deliberately undermined by references to extraordinary rendition and the detention center at Guantanamo Bay. These examples reveal the gap between America’s idealized self-image and the actions carried out by its government, military personnel, or foreign partners. The author criticizes efforts to treat abuses as isolated acts committed by a few individuals while ignoring the broader policies and institutions that enabled or sanctioned mistreatment.

Through pointed rhetorical questions, the text exposes the hypocrisy of preserving a virtuous national identity by denying responsibility whenever American personnel or proxies commit abuse. Its central argument is that a nation cannot credibly condemn figures like Graner as exceptions while refusing to confront the systems, policies, and official decisions that made such conduct possible.
outputs.L4:
The passage uses biting irony and a series of rhetorical questions to dismantle the claim that Charles Graner’s abuses at Abu Ghraib were merely the actions of one exceptionally cruel soldier. Graner may be portrayed as a sadist and an aberration, but the passage refuses to let the United States distance itself so easily from what he did. Its questions force readers to consider whether the humiliation, degradation, and torture of prisoners can honestly be separated from the policies, institutions, and political climate that made such conduct possible.

This denial becomes especially unconvincing when set beside other features of the post-9/11 “war on terror.” The passage invokes extraordinary rendition, through which detainees were transferred to countries known to use torture, as well as the detention and interrogation practices associated with Guantanamo Bay. These examples suggest that Abu Ghraib was not an isolated moral failure occurring outside official policy. Even when American authorities did not directly inflict abuse, they created legal categories, secret procedures, and chains of custody that allowed coercion and suffering to occur while preserving a degree of plausible deniability.

The irony lies in America’s effort to maintain an image of itself as a nation fundamentally opposed to torture while treating each revelation of abuse as an exception. By repeatedly asking, in effect, how a country can condemn Graner while defending rendition, indefinite detention, and coercive interrogation, the passage exposes the contradiction between national ideals and state practices. Graner becomes a convenient scapegoat: his evident cruelty makes it possible to locate responsibility in one deviant personality rather than in the broader system that authorized, encouraged, tolerated, or concealed abuse.

The passage therefore does not excuse Graner’s individual guilt. Instead, it argues that focusing exclusively on his sadism narrows responsibility too much. His actions must be understood within a larger structure involving military command, intelligence practices, legal justifications, and public fear. The central accusation is that systemic complicity cannot be erased by punishing a few visible offenders. If torture was enabled by national policy and carried out in America’s name, then the country must confront not only the conduct of one man but also the institutions and assumptions that made his conduct possible.
outputs.L5:
### Charles Graner and the Abu Ghraib Scandal

Charles Graner is a former U.S. Army reservist known for his role in the abuse of detainees at Abu Ghraib prison in Iraq. Photographs taken inside the facility showed Graner and other military personnel humiliating and mistreating prisoners, prompting international condemnation and investigations into detention practices during the Iraq War.

In 2005, a military court convicted Graner of offenses including assault, conspiracy, maltreatment of detainees, and committing indecent acts. He received a ten-year prison sentence and was later released after serving approximately six and a half years. The case helped generate broader debate about military accountability, command responsibility, and the treatment of prisoners. It also demonstrated why governments must not let wartime conditions weaken legal and ethical standards.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a biting satirical monologue arguing that Charles Graner’s abuse at Abu Ghraib cannot be separated from America’s broader policies of torture, rendition, and denial. Use repetition, rhetorical questions, and the refrain “Charles Graner is not America.”
counterfactuals.output:
“Charles Graner is not America.”

Of course not. America is much larger. America has letterhead.

Charles Graner had a leash. America had legal memoranda. Charles Graner had photographs. America had classified annexes. Charles Graner grinned beside naked prisoners; America frowned gravely behind a podium and announced that the photographs did not reflect “our values.”

Charles Graner is not America.

America does not torture. America merely redefines pain. America does not disappear people. America conducts “extraordinary rendition.” America does not run secret prisons. America maintains “black sites,” which are entirely different because the sign outside is invisible. America does not evade the Geneva Conventions. America consults lawyers until the Conventions become suggestions, the suggestions become ambiguities, and the ambiguities become permission.

But Charles Graner? A bad apple. A lone aberration. A spontaneous storm in a perfectly clear policy climate.

Charles Graner is not America.

Who wrote the memos? Not Graner. Who approved coercive interrogation techniques? Not Graner. Who built the machinery that moved captives across borders, beyond courts, beyond lawyers, beyond public sight? Not Graner. Who insisted, year after year, that abuse was isolated while the same vocabulary—stress positions, sleep deprivation, sensory manipulation—echoed from one detention site to another?

Surely that was all Graner too. A remarkably busy man. A night-shift reservist with the power to draft doctrine, coordinate agencies, negotiate foreign cooperation, classify evidence, and teach an empire how to look away.

Charles Graner is not America.

No, America is the clean hand pointing at the dirty hand. America is the solemn inquiry with the narrow mandate. America is the redacted page explaining that transparency requires darkness. America is the official saying, “We do not torture,” followed by a footnote defining torture as something that, by definition, we do not do.

See how beautifully the logic works?

If a prisoner is beaten by a rogue guard, it is misconduct.  
If a prisoner is broken by an approved technique, it is policy.  
If a prisoner is flown to another country to be broken, it is diplomacy.  
If no one is prosecuted at the top, it is healing.  
If someone at the bottom goes to prison, it is accountability.

Charles Graner is not America.

He was punished, and therefore the system was innocent. The photograph was condemned, and therefore the room that produced it vanished. The uniform was disgraced, and therefore the suits were absolved. We found the villain exactly where power prefers to find villains: low enough to prosecute, visible enough to hate, crude enough to make everyone above him look refined.

Was Graner responsible for his actions? Yes. Was his cruelty real? Yes. Does individual guilt erase institutional design? Only in the grand national theater where responsibility flows downhill and exoneration rises like steam.

Charles Graner is not America.

He did not invent the euphemism. He did not authorize the architecture. He did not create the culture in which human beings became “detainees,” suffering became “pressure,” and law became an obstacle to be interpreted into obedience. He did not make denial a national sacrament: first deny the act, then deny the pattern, then deny the policy, then praise ourselves for investigating what we have already decided cannot be true.

Charles Graner is not America.

He is merely the face America was willing to put on the policy—the face coarse enough to condemn, small enough to cage, and useful enough to preserve the fiction that Abu Ghraib was a basement with no upstairs.

So repeat it. Repeat it until the memos bleach white, until the flight logs blow away, until the black sites fade into patriotic mist.

“Charles Graner is not America.”

No. He is not America.

He is what America photographed—and what America cropped out.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an ironic political essay about Abu Ghraib in which the narrator repeatedly insists that “America does not torture,” while gradually exposing the hypocrisy of that claim through references to Charles Graner, Guantanamo, and extraordinary rendition.
counterfactuals.output:
### America Does Not Torture

America does not torture.

This is important to remember when looking at the photographs from Abu Ghraib. The hooded man standing on a box, wires trailing from his hands, was not being tortured. He was participating in an improvised electrical-safety demonstration. The naked prisoners stacked into a human pyramid were not being tortured either. They were assisting with an architectural experiment conducted under difficult wartime conditions.

The dogs, the leashes, the forced poses, the terror on prisoners’ faces—none of these should distract us from the governing principle: America does not torture.

Charles Graner understood this principle. A military policeman later convicted for his role in the abuse, Graner appeared in several of the photographs, smiling with the confidence of a man who knew that language would arrive afterward to tidy up what the camera had recorded. Bruises could be renamed “pressure.” Humiliation could become “softening up.” Terror could be filed under “enhanced interrogation.” If a prisoner died, there were always forms to complete and passive verbs to deploy.

Mistakes were made. Procedures were violated. Standards were not upheld. Bodies, apparently, abused themselves.

America does not torture.

Graner was sentenced to prison, which proved that the system worked. The system worked so well that responsibility settled largely on a handful of low-ranking soldiers, as if the policies, memoranda, legal theories, intelligence demands, and command pressures hovering above Abu Ghraib had merely been weather. A few bad apples had appeared spontaneously in a barrel designed, supervised, shipped, and stored by no one in particular.

It was comforting to blame the photographs. Without photographs, after all, there might have been only testimony, and testimony from prisoners is notoriously inconvenient. A photograph cannot easily be told that it misunderstood the question, harbored anti-American bias, or belonged to an unlawful enemy organization. So the photographs became the scandal—not necessarily what they showed, but the fact that they showed it.

Fortunately, Abu Ghraib was an aberration. Guantanamo was entirely different.

At Guantanamo Bay, detainees were placed beyond the ordinary protections of American courts because America is a nation of laws. They were called “enemy combatants” because familiar legal categories might have brought familiar legal rights. Interrogation methods were reviewed, authorized, revised, suspended, and occasionally authorized again. Sleep deprivation, stress positions, isolation, sensory manipulation, forced nudity, and exposure to extreme temperatures occupied the clean administrative space between cruelty and whatever officials were prepared to call torture.

America does not torture. It develops techniques.

Some detainees were chained in painful positions. Others were kept awake until thought itself began to fray. One could say that these practices were intended to break the prisoner’s resistance, but “break” sounds violent. Better to say they encouraged cooperation. Better still to say they produced intelligence, even when the intelligence was false, recycled, or offered merely to make the suffering stop.

And if Guantanamo’s legal geography became awkward, there remained extraordinary rendition.

“Extraordinary” is a useful word. It lends glamour to logistics. A man is seized, blindfolded, diapered, shackled, placed aboard an aircraft, and delivered to a government known for brutal interrogation. This is not outsourcing torture. America does not torture. It merely transports certain questions to countries where answers are extracted according to local custom.

The planes had flight plans. The captors had paperwork. The receiving prisons had cells. Bureaucracy moved with admirable precision, allowing conscience to be divided into manageable departments. One country supplied the prisoner, another supplied the room, another supplied the interrogators, and everyone supplied deniability.

America does not torture; it renders.

Perhaps this is the real achievement of the post-September 11 vocabulary. It taught a democracy to speak about cruelty without naming it. Waterboarding became a technique. Secret prisons became black sites. Kidnapping became rendition. Indefinite detention became a necessary precaution. And torture, when performed by allies, became intelligence cooperation.

The insistence was always categorical: America does not torture. The evidence was always conditional: except when the victim was dangerous, except when the danger was urgent, except when lawyers had narrowed the definition, except when another country held the instruments, except when the photographs were misunderstood, except when the people involved had been frightened since September 11.

A principle with enough exceptions begins to resemble a permission slip.

Abu Ghraib was shocking not because it revealed an America no one could imagine, but because it made official euphemisms suddenly visible. The photographs translated policy back into flesh. “Stress position” became a man collapsing. “Humiliation” became a leash around a neck. “Interrogation environment” became a corridor in which prisoners feared dogs, fists, wires, and the laughter of their guards.

Charles Graner’s grin was especially damaging because it lacked the solemnity of a legal memorandum. It did not claim necessity. It did not cite executive power. It simply recorded pleasure and impunity in the same frame.

Still, America does not torture.

America prosecutes a guard, classifies a document, redraws a legal boundary, commissions a report, and waits for the public memory to soften. It condemns cruelty in the abstract and debates each concrete instance until the victim disappears beneath definitions. It assures the world that its values remain intact, provided no one looks too closely at the places where those values were tested.

America does not torture.

It only did things that looked like torture, felt like torture, produced the injuries of torture, required the secrecy of torture, and demanded the legal evasions of torture.

But the word itself was never authorized.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: In a sarcastic, confrontational voice, write a short commentary contrasting Charles Graner’s personal cruelty—domestic violence, prisoner abuse, and grotesque emails—with America’s self-image as morally innocent.
counterfactuals.output: America loves to picture itself as the spotless hero, forever shocked that cruelty exists anywhere near its flag. Then there’s Charles Graner: accused of brutal domestic violence, convicted for abusing prisoners at Abu Ghraib, and author of grotesque emails treating humiliation like a punch line. But sure, keep polishing the halo. Graner wasn’t some alien contaminant; he was an American guard empowered inside an American-run prison. The real obscenity is pretending his cruelty appeared from nowhere—and vanished the moment the photographs became inconvenient.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a darkly humorous rant that uses Charles Graner as a symbol of American denial after the Abu Ghraib scandal. Include “Am I right?” several times and end by challenging the reader’s belief that Graner’s actions were un-American.
counterfactuals.output:
Charles Graner became America’s favorite kind of monster: the kind we can put in a uniform, lock in a cell, and pretend arrived from another planet. Problem solved! National conscience disinfected! Am I right?

Because nothing says accountability like blaming a few grinning reservists while everyone farther up the chain discovers a sudden, debilitating allergy to responsibility. Graner was “a bad apple,” they said, as though bad apples routinely receive legal memos, institutional secrecy, and a bureaucracy willing to rename torture “enhanced interrogation.” Am I right?

We looked at those photographs with the horror of people catching their own reflection in a dark window. Then we immediately decided it was someone else standing there. That wasn’t America. That was Graner. That wasn’t policy. That was misconduct. That wasn’t a system. That was one sadist with a camera and apparently the supernatural ability to invent an entire climate of dehumanization by himself. Am I right?

Graner became the perfect patriotic scapegoat: guilty enough to punish, low-ranking enough to discard, and visible enough to absorb every uncomfortable question. We could sentence him, denounce him, and go back to believing cruelty only counts when it embarrasses us publicly.

So by all means, call Graner a disgrace. Call his actions criminal, grotesque, and cruel. But before you call them un-American, ask yourself: were they truly alien to America—or merely American behavior we could no longer keep outside the frame?
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a polemical prose passage about U.S. torture policy that repeatedly personifies America as a husband and father, insists Graner “is not America,” and uses escalating irony to implicate the nation in the abuses it officially disavows.
counterfactuals.output:
America is a husband who comes home late with blood on his cuff and asks why dinner is cold. America is a father who lectures the children about decency, then locks the basement door and turns up the radio. When photographs leak from the dark—hoods, wires, leashes, grinning custodians of the republic—he points to one face and says: Graner is not America.

Graner is not America. America merely wrote the rules vaguely enough for Graner to misunderstand them. America merely sent him into a prison where cruelty descended the chain of command like an heirloom: polished upstairs, handled downstairs, denied everywhere. America merely renamed pain “enhanced interrogation,” renamed captivity “detention,” renamed human beings “detainees,” and then expressed shock that its servants became fluent in the national euphemism.

Graner is not America. America is the husband who never struck anyone; his hand only approved the memorandum. America is the father who never ordered humiliation; he only explained that the law had become inconvenient. He stands before the family portrait, grave and injured, insisting that whatever happened in the basement was the work of a few bad children—children he trained, armed, supervised, rewarded, and abandoned when the flashbulb went off.

Certainly Graner is not America. America is cleaner than that. America wears a suit. America does not pose beside the damaged body; America convenes a hearing. America does not snarl for the camera; America lowers its voice, invokes security, and classifies the evidence. America does not torture; America discovers, after careful review, that torture occurred in places it controlled, under authorities it created, for purposes it demanded, but without ever becoming policy in the impolite sense of the word.

Graner is not America. He is only the alibi America handcuffed to the scandal. He is the disposable face pasted over a system so the system may continue faceless. Punish the hand, preserve the signature. Condemn the photograph, protect the room. Tell the children their father is honorable because he prosecuted the man who carried out what no honorable father would admit he had made possible.

And when America comes home again, smelling of antiseptic and secrecy, he gathers the family close. He tells them monsters live elsewhere. He tells them law is our shield and mercy our inheritance. He tells them Graner is not America.

Then, from behind the locked door, someone begins to scream—and America, exemplary husband, vigilant father, turns up the anthem.
